title: Benchmark parallel vs sequential for a list of 10 elements vs 10 million elements and explain the overhead.
shortTitle: Benchmark parallel vs sequential for 10 elements vs 10 million and explain the overhead
topicTitle: Benchmark parallel vs sequential for a list of 10 elements vs 10 million element

s1_definition.profdef: A rough benchmark times a sequential and a parallel reduction over small and large lists. For ten elements the parallel version is slower due to fixed split/merge overhead; for ten million it is usually faster because the work dwarfs the overhead.
s1_definition.analogy: Hiring extra clerks to total a three-line ledger wastes time coordinating them, but for a million-line ledger the extra clerks finish far sooner.
s1_definition.oneliner: Parallel loses on tiny inputs (overhead dominates) and wins on huge inputs (work dominates).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A rough benchmark times a sequential and a parallel reduction over small and large lists. For ten elements the parallel version is slower due to fixed split/merge overhead; for ten million it is usually faster because the work dwarfs the overhead.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Hiring extra clerks to total a three-line ledger wastes time coordinating them, but for a million-line ledger the extra clerks finish far sooner.

**One line to remember:** Parallel loses on tiny inputs (overhead dominates) and wins on huge inputs (work dominates).

sections.s2_technical:
You time `list.stream().mapToLong(...).sum()` versus `list.parallelStream().mapToLong(...).sum()` for n equal to ten and n equal to ten million, using `System.nanoTime` around each. Parallelism has a fixed cost: splitting the source, scheduling tasks on the ForkJoinPool, and merging partial results. For tiny n this fixed cost exceeds the actual work, so sequential wins. For huge n the per-element work across many cores far exceeds the overhead, so parallel wins.

A rough timing loop is illustrative, though a proper micro-benchmark uses JMH to account for JIT warm-up and avoid dead-code elimination. The crossover point depends on element cost, core count, and source splittability.

The senior nuance is that a hand-rolled nanoTime benchmark is only indicative — JIT warm-up, garbage collection, and dead-code elimination can mislead, so I use JMH for real numbers. The lesson stands regardless: parallelism is not free, and I only apply it after measuring with representative data. I also note that the crossover is lower when per-element work is expensive and higher when it is trivial like adding.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India decides whether to parallelise a salary-sum job by comparing timings on a tiny and a huge dataset.

This is exactly what the small-versus-large benchmark shows — the overhead hurts on ten elements and helps on ten million.

The code defines a `BenchmarkService timing both and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a list of ten longs and a list of ten million longs.

Step 1: For ten elements, the sequential sum finishes almost instantly on one thread.

Step 2: The parallel sum must split, schedule, and merge for just ten elements, so its fixed overhead makes it slower.

Step 3: For ten million elements, the sequential sum must walk them all on one thread.

Step 4: The parallel sum spreads the work across cores, and because the total work dwarfs the overhead, it finishes faster — illustrating the crossover.

```
INFO: n=10 → sequential=1500ns  parallel=250000ns
INFO: n=10,000,000 → sequential=38000000ns  parallel=12000000ns
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  n=10:        seq (1 thread, tiny)      < par (split/merge overhead) → sequential wins
  n=10,000,000: seq (1 thread, all work) > par (split across cores)   → parallel wins
     overhead is fixed; benefit grows with n
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Parallel Benchmark Decision ═══

  measure seq vs par on representative sizes

```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — parallel overhead vs benefit ═══

  ┌─ fixed cost vs scaling work ───────────────────────────────┐
  │ parallel fixed cost: split + schedule(ForkJoinPool) + merge│
  │ n=10: overhead >> work → sequential faster                 │
  │ n=10M: work >> overhead → parallel faster (crossover)      │
  │ crossover depends on element cost, cores, splittability     │
  │ nanoTime = indicative; use JMH for real numbers            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │          BenchmarkService     │
  │  + compare(log, label, data)    │ time seq vs par
  │  - time(Runnable): long          │ nanoTime (indicative)
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. time(sequential sum) vs time(parallel sum)
  2. compare across n=10 and n=10M
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To decide whether parallelism pays off I time a sequential sum against a parallel sum on both a tiny list of ten elements and a huge list of ten million. For ten elements the parallel version is slower, because parallelism has a fixed cost — splitting the source, scheduling tasks on the ForkJoinPool, and merging the partial results — and for such a small input that fixed cost dwarfs the actual work. For ten million elements the parallel version is usually faster, because spreading the work across cores saves far more time than the overhead costs. That is the crossover.

I am careful to flag that a hand-rolled nanoTime timing is only indicative, because JIT warm-up, garbage collection, and dead-code elimination can all distort the numbers, so for real measurements I use JMH, which handles warm-up and prevents the optimiser from discarding unused results. At the National Bank of India I would use this comparison to decide whether to parallelise a salary-sum job.

The senior point I stress is that parallelism is never free, so I only apply it after measuring with representative data. The crossover point is not fixed — it is lower when each element involves expensive work and higher when the per-element operation is as trivial as an addition. The lesson I take away is to measure, not guess, and to default to sequential unless the data is large and the measured parallel version actually wins.
